amendments.rule: A `noncompositional` unit under rules 39 and 45 never absorbs an intervening **article**: the article contributes no part of the fused English word, so it stays its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 23. `ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν` → *henceforth* joins the preposition and the adverb and leaves `τοῦ` empty, as `εἰς τὸ πάλιν` leaves its own article empty at 2CO.13.2. Not one of the corpus's 102 `noncompositional` units contains an article token, so this is not a judgment call. What **is** a judgment call is which of the two the phrase is, and rule 34 against rule 45 decides it on the English: where the adverb's own ordinary gloss already spells the whole English word, the preposition is pleonastic and is `unrepresented` with the adverb taking the word alone, which is why 2CO.13.2 gives *again* to `πάλιν` and nothing to `εἰς`; where the English word carries a sense the adverb alone does not, the preposition is in it and rule 45 joins the pair, which is why `νῦν` — *now* in 54 of its 62 corpus units and never *henceforth* — cannot take *henceforth* by itself. Decide that from what the corpus spends on the adverb, as rule 91 decides a head, and say in the note where the phrase is unattested. The article's status is unaffected either way. That judgment call is scoped to a governed **adverb**, which is a word able to spell an English adverb by itself, and the pleonastic arm is not available at all where the governed word is a **noun** and the single English word the ASV writes is an **adverb**: a noun does not spell an adverb, the adverbial force being what the preposition and the case contribute, so rule 94's count test makes the pair one unit and rule 39's test keeps it `aligned` wherever part of the English answers to the noun's own lexeme, headed on the noun. `ἐν τάχει` → *quickly*, *shortly* and *speedily* is one `aligned` unit on the dative noun in every corpus unit that writes the preposition — 1TI.3.14, REV.1.1, ROM.16.20 and LUK.18.8 — and not one leaves `ἐν` `unrepresented`, the bare `τάχει` taking the word alone only where the Greek writes no preposition, as REV.22.6 does. Do not read a cognate Greek **adverb** the ASV renders by that same English word — `ταχέως` → *shortly*, *quickly*, *hastily* — as evidence that the noun spells it by itself: that is evidence of the opposite, the adverb being where the corpus spends the bare English adverb and the noun being what needs the preposition to reach it.
amendments.why: Rule 93 states the 34-versus-45 test entirely in terms of a governed adverb (`νῦν`, `πάλιν`), and ACT.12.7 met the case it had not considered: a governed **noun** whose phrase the ASV renders by a single English adverb. Read literally, the existing test invites the pleonastic reading — quickly looks like the ordinary gloss of the τάχος family — and that is the reading ACT.12.7 originally took. The evidence refuses it: all four corpus units of `ἐν τάχει` join the pair as one `aligned` unit headed on the noun (1TI.3.14, REV.1.1, ROM.16.20, LUK.18.8), REV.22.6 keeps the word on a bare `τάχει` only because no preposition is written, and the eight units of the cognate adverb `ταχέως` show that *quickly*, *shortly* and *hastily* are what the corpus spends on the adverb rather than the noun. Two of those `ἐν τάχει` notes had already weighed the rule 34 reading and rejected it for exactly this reason, so the corpus is unanimous and self-consistent, and the amendment records what it already does rather than inventing a line. Amended rather than added as a new rule so that the sentence a verse pass reads first is the corrected one; the rest of rule 93's text, including its article clause and its instruction to note an unattested phrase, is preserved verbatim.

conventions: Where the ASV renders a Greek participle by an English participle, that participle licenses no supplied subject word: an English participle has no subject slot, so a supplied he or they standing in front of it belongs to the finite verb whose subject it is, discontinuously under rule 15. 12.17 gives κατασείσας a bare beckoning and he … declared to διηγήσατο. A participle the ASV renders finite is the contrast and takes the supplied subject itself, as at 12.9, 12.10, 12.12, 12.16, 12.19 and 12.25, and a genitive absolute whose own pronoun is expressed gives the subject word to that pronoun, as 12.13 gives he to αὐτοῦ while 12.18, having no pronoun, leaves the supplied it with the participle. Decide it by which verb the supplied subject is the subject of, never by the ASV's word order.

ἐπικαλέω in the ASV's whose surname was X frame heads on surname, which is the word glossing the lexeme under rule 91; the copula rides along under rule 9 and the relativizing pronoun stays on the substantival article under rule 32 (12.12, 12.25).

This chapter's several Greek verbs the ASV renders by a support frame whose supplied noun carries the sense are headed on that noun throughout, under rule 17: σιγᾶν -> to hold their peace on peace (12.17), ἀπαχθῆναι -> be put to death on death (12.19), ἐδημηγόρει -> made an oration on oration (12.21), ἐξέψυξεν -> gave up the ghost on ghost (12.23), πείσαντες -> made … their friend on friend (12.20). A compound Greek word whose English words each gloss one of its elements is the contrast and heads on the core under rule 66: θυμομαχῶν on displeased, ὁμοθυμαδόν on accord, σκωληκόβρωτος on eaten, διϊσχυρίζετο on affirmed. Ask first whether any English word glosses the lexeme at all.

report: Checked all 44 candidate lemma groups and read the dump end to end for the added/folded asymmetries the keyed table cannot see. Two genuine problems; everything else is the ASV rendering one word differently in contexts the source licenses.

ACT.12.7 ἐν τάχει: corrected, and this is what the evidence round was for. All four τάχος units that write the preposition join it to the noun as one aligned unit on the single English word (1TI.3.14, REV.1.1, ROM.16.20 shortly; LUK.18.8 speedily), τάχει standing alone only at REV.22.6 where the Greek writes no preposition; and the eight ταχέως units show that quickly, shortly and hastily are where the corpus spends the bare English adverb. The noun does not spell the adverb by itself, so the rule 34 pleonastic reading fails rule 93's own test. The pair is now one aligned unit on quickly, headed on τάχει.

ACT.12.3 τῶν ἀζύμων: corrected — a real intra-chapter split. At 12.20 τῆς βασιλικῆς -> the … country gives the determiner and the supplied nominal to the article under rule 102, while 12.3 left its article unrepresented and kept the supplied bread with the adjective. Rule 17's generic-noun clause is scoped in terms to anarthrous Greek; rule 49's τὸ τρίτον -> the third part and οἱ ἡμέτεροι -> our people give the nominal to the article with or without a written determiner; and rule 102's REV.11.15 τοῦ κυρίου -> the kingdom of puts the case preposition there too. So τῶν now takes the discontinuous of … bread headed on bread, and ἀζύμων keeps a bare unleavened, which rule 66's generic-completion test had already made the right head.

BSB: of the ten flags, nine are documented convention differences and stand — τῇ at 12.6 (rule 38's multiword determiner clause), αἱ at 12.7 (rule 20 displacement), the four articles the ASV gives no determiner at 12.1, 12.12, 12.14 and 12.20 (rules 21 and 23), the interrogative ἄρα at 12.18 (rule 64), the rule 97 surplus εἰς at 12.25, and the ἐπί the ASV compresses into chamberlain at 12.20. The tenth, ἐν at 12.7, is the genuine error and is patched; the BSB flag and the corpus agree there.

Checked and found consistent, with nothing to change: rule 106's accusative arm across six verbs (12.7 on, 12.10 through, 12.13 at, 12.19 for, 12.20 for, 12.21 in); the preverb-versus-preposition division (12.7 and 12.17 write both words and split, 12.10 writes one and gives it to the expressed ἀπό); the periphrastic ἦν plus participle split in all four instances (12.5, 12.6, 12.12, 12.20); rule 20's second arm used only where no possessor token stands (12.1, 12.7, 12.25) against seven rule 20 displacements; the three τε units under rule 70; every article before a name; rule 58's supplied determiner on the expressed noun (12.10, 12.21); and the supplied-word folds under rule 103 (12.4, 12.7, 12.12, 12.19, 12.22), whose only added counterpart in the chapter is the rule 97 case at 12.25.

12.18's was become of keeps the of inside ἐγένετο's unit because Πέτρος is nominative and English writes no preposition to realize that case. That is one unit only and I have not promoted it: rule 21's own wording — a preposition realizing the governed word's own case — already reaches it, and a nominative clause bolted onto rule 106's preverb rule would be a rule built on one instance.
Both corpus requests from the previous round were answered and both bore on the same unit. No requests remain.
